name: Escalation of commitment
statement: Someone who chose a failing course of action commits more resources to it than someone handed the same failing course by another person.
meaning: Escalation of commitment is a claim about who made the first decision. Two managers face the same project, the same losses and the same budget. One picked the project; the other inherited it from a predecessor. The claim is that the first will put more money in. That makes escalation narrower than the sunk-cost effect, which is about the size of the unrecoverable outlay and is indifferent to who spent it. It also requires bad news. Sleesman and colleagues, defining the literature for their meta-analysis, admitted only studies in which decision makers continued a failing course of action, and excluded sunk-cost studies with no negative feedback.

origin.note: The paper is "Knee-deep in the big muddy: a study of escalating commitment to a chosen course of action", volume 16, pages 27 to 44. Sleesman and colleagues note that the title borrows from Pete Seeger's 1967 Vietnam protest song "Waist Deep in the Big Muddy". Staw's own framing was the war: he quotes a July 1965 memo from George Ball to Lyndon Johnson, taken from the Pentagon Papers, warning that heavy casualties would start a well-nigh irreversible process.

evidence: Staw recruited 240 undergraduates from the College of Commerce and Business Administration at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign. Playing a financial vice president in 1967, subjects sent 10 million dollars of research funding to one of two divisions of the Adams & Smith Company, Consumer Products or Industrial Products. Five years on in the case, with 20 million dollars now to split as they liked, they allocated again. Half were shown figures in which the division they backed had recovered, half figures in which it had gone on losing. Half never made the first decision at all: they were told a previous officer had made it. One subject could not pick a division at the first step and was dropped, leaving 239 in the analysis and 235 degrees of freedom for error. The two halves were not built the same way. The 120 low-responsibility subjects were assigned 30 to each of four cells, while the 120 high-responsibility subjects chose their own division, 64 taking Consumer Products and 55 Industrial. The measure was money sent to the previously chosen division. Under high personal responsibility subjects gave it 11.08 million on average, against 8.89 million under low responsibility. Under negative consequences they gave 11.20 million, against 8.77 million under positive consequences. Both main effects were significant, F(1, 235) = 14.40 and F(1, 235) = 17.93, p < .001, and so was the interaction, F(1, 235) = 5.56, p < .019. The cell that carries the paper is high responsibility with negative consequences, where the average allocation was 13.07 million, and Staw reports it as the only cell differing significantly from the other three.

replication.headline: Pooled across 54 samples and 8,625 units the responsibility effect holds, and both direct repeats of Staw's own experiment failed to reproduce the interaction it was built on.
replication.detail: Sleesman, Conlon, McNamara and Miles worked from an initial list of 917 articles and kept 166 independent samples. Personal responsibility for the initial decision correlated with escalation at a corrected rho of .258 across 54 samples and 8,625 units, 95% CI .216 to .301, with a fail-safe N of 225. Sunk costs gave rho = .243 across 34 samples and 5,524 units, CI .114 to .373, and proximity to project completion gave rho = .393 across 14 samples and 3,073 units, CI .308 to .478. Fourteen of their 16 main-effect predictions held. One moderator test bears directly on Staw's mechanism and came out null: responsibility predicted escalation at rho = .289 across the 32 samples where the first decision was explicitly chosen and .238 across the 19 where it was assigned, intervals .236 to .343 and .164 to .311. The aggregate is not the 1976 experiment, and two teams have run that experiment again. Białek, Węgrzyn and Meyers recruited 425 Polish speakers and analysed 365 after dropping the fastest and the slowest, giving them Staw's vignette in Polish. Personal responsibility did nothing, F(1, 357) = 0.05, p = 0.828, and neither did the interaction, F(1, 357) = 0.15, p = 0.704. Feedback moved money towards the division that was doing well, F(1, 357) = 5.69, p = 0.018, a direction their discussion calls the reverse of Staw's and their results section calls consistent with it. Dhanda, Ziano and colleagues then ran a preregistered close replication on Amazon Mechanical Turk in November 2018, recruiting 403 and analysing 400. Responsibility came out as Staw had it, F(1, 396) = 16.39, p < .001, partial eta squared 0.040, d = 0.41, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.60. Consequences came out backwards, with positive consequences drawing more money than negative, d = 0.53, and the interaction was absent, F(1, 396) = 1.20, p = .273. Their third study repeated Wong and Kwong's escalation scenario on 595 recruited and 568 analysed participants and found no responsibility effect at all, F(1, 564) = 0.74, p = .39. The responsibility effect turned up in one of those three tests, and Staw's interaction in none.

study.cite: Dhanda, N., Ziano, I., Ching, K. H., Phuong, A. K. L., Lo, Y. T., Yip, M. K., Shi, B. J., & Cheng, B. (2026). A Replication and Extension of Three Studies Investigating Escalation of Commitment and Regret Aversion. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 52(9), 2677-2692.

limits: Staw reports means and F ratios and no standardised effect. The 0.49 above is Dhanda and colleagues' conversion of his figures, made to power their replication, and it is not a number in his paper. The evidence base is also thinner in the field than the pooled figures suggest. Of the 54 responsibility samples in the meta-analysis, 50 were laboratory studies at rho = .277 and four were not at rho = .178, and Sleesman and colleagues could not run the same comparison on sunk costs or project completion for want of non-laboratory studies. What field work exists disagrees with itself. Staw and Hoang followed 241 players taken in the first two rounds of the 1980 to 1986 drafts who signed contracts and lasted two seasons. Draft number still predicted minutes played in the second year, 22.77 fewer minutes per place, after controls for prior scoring, toughness, quickness, injury, trade, position and team record, and it still predicted them in year five at 13.77, on one-tailed tests. A separate survival sample of 275 players yielded 184 exits, and each increment in draft number raised the hazard of being cut by 3 per cent. Camerer and Weber did not rework those data. They collected 229 players from the 1986 to 1991 drafts, reproduced the finding, then used a two-stage procedure to strip out the information draft order carries about future performance. The escalation effect survived in years two and three at roughly half the size, which they read as firmer evidence for it. Leeds, Leeds and Motomura took the 409 players drafted between 1995 and 2005 who signed a contract and played 500 minutes in some season, and looked for a jump in playing time at the lottery and first-round thresholds. They found none, and say so against Staw and Hoang by name. Staw, Barsade and Koput followed 132 Californian banks over nine years and found executive turnover predicting provisions for loan losses and write-offs, with no effect in the reverse direction; only their abstract could be obtained. Whether any of this holds when the money is real is not settled here. Martens and Orzen rebuilt the design with the incentive protocols of experimental economics, and report in their abstract that subjects responded to negative feedback differently when it carried a financial loss and when they had made the initial investment. Their full text could not be obtained, so no figure of theirs appears above. One moderator in the meta-analysis deserves its own warning: sunk costs predicted escalation at rho = .528 in the five samples that bundled sunk cost with information about how near completion the project was, and at rho = .100, CI -.036 to .236, in the 28 samples that did not.
misreadings: Escalation is not a synonym for the sunk-cost effect, which this atlas covers at number 1, though the two entries share most of their literature. Sunk cost asks whether money already spent moves the decision. Escalation asks whether having been the one who spent it moves the decision further, and it needs the project to be visibly failing. The second error is the one this entry exists for. "Escalation replicates" and "Staw 1976 replicates" are separate claims, and only the first is comfortable: a meta-analysis of 54 samples supports the responsibility effect, while both attempts to rerun the original found no interaction and a consequences effect pointing the wrong way. Third, persistence alone is not escalation. Continuing a project that still looks worth finishing is a forecast, right or wrong, rather than a bias, and Sleesman and colleagues excluded studies without negative feedback for that reason. They also excluded commitment to the status quo, which has its own entry at number 51, because staying put is not the same as putting more in. Fourth, Staw's paper is often read as showing that people throw good money after bad in general. It showed that one group of students did so, and the effect he reported was concentrated in a single cell of four.

sources.text: Staw, B. M. (1976). Knee-deep in the big muddy: a study of escalating commitment to a chosen course of action. Organizational Behavior and Human Performance, 16(1), 27-44. Every figure quoted here was read from the text of the article itself, hosted at San Jose State University.

Sleesman, D. J., Conlon, D. E., McNamara, G., & Miles, J. E. (2012). Cleaning Up the Big Muddy: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Determinants of Escalation of Commitment. Academy of Management Journal, 55(3), 541-562. Tables 2 and 3 were read from the full text of the published article, hosted at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology, which the url points to; the publisher's own page is paywalled.

Białek, M., Węgrzyn, M., & Meyers, E. A. (2021). Escalation of commitment is independent of numeracy and cognitive reflection. Failed replication and extension of Staw (1976). Economics and Business Review, 7(2), 5-16. Open access; 425 recruited and 365 analysed. The vignette was translated from Staw but the replication drops his requirement that high-responsibility subjects write a paragraph defending the first choice.

Dhanda, N., Ziano, I., Ching, K. H., Phuong, A. K. L., Lo, Y. T., Yip, M. K., Shi, B. J., & Cheng, B. (2026). A Replication and Extension of Three Studies Investigating Escalation of Commitment and Regret Aversion. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 52(9), 2677-2692. Published online 19 June 2025 and open access under CC-BY; the figures here were read from the deposited full text at PubMed Central. Study 1 is a preregistered close replication of Staw (1976) and Study 3 replicates Wong and Kwong (2007). The authors note that their Study 1 data violate normality, W = 0.99, p < .001.

Staw, B. M., & Hoang, H. (1995). Sunk Costs in the NBA: Why Draft Order Affects Playing Time and Survival in Professional Basketball. Administrative Science Quarterly, 40(3), 474-494. Read from a scan of the article; the playing-time and survival analyses use different samples, 241 players and 275 players.

Camerer, C. F., & Weber, R. A. (1999). The econometrics and behavioral economics of escalation of commitment: a re-examination of Staw and Hoang's NBA data. Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, 39(1), 59-82. The published article is paywalled, so the figures here were read from the authors' working paper of August 1998, Caltech Social Science Working Paper 1043, which the url points to.

Leeds, D., Leeds, M. A., & Motomura, A. (2015). Are Sunk Costs Irrelevant? Evidence from Playing Time in the National Basketball Association. Economic Inquiry, 53(2), 1305-1316. The published version is paywalled; the figures here were read from the authors' Temple University working paper DETU 13-04 of November 2013, which the url points to.

Staw, B. M., Barsade, S. G., & Koput, K. W. (1997). Escalation at the credit window: A longitudinal study of bank executives' recognition and write-off of problem loans. Journal of Applied Psychology, 82(1), 130-142. The full text could not be obtained. Crossref carries no abstract for it, and the sentence on this page is taken from the abstract deposited in the University of Arizona research repository.

Martens, N., & Orzen, H. (2021). Escalating commitment to a failing course of action, a re-examination. European Economic Review, 137, 103811. The full text could not be obtained and no repository copy was located through Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar or the second author's departmental page. The sentence on this page comes from the abstract, read at both Semantic Scholar and RePEc; no figure from it is quoted.

Sleesman, D. J., Lennard, A. C., McNamara, G., & Conlon, D. E. (2018). Putting Escalation of Commitment in Context: A Multilevel Review and Analysis. Academy of Management Annals, 12(1), 178-207. Listed because it is the field's standing review and Białek and colleagues cite it for the published record. Its full text could not be obtained and nothing on this page rests on it.
